nodeData.note: The first three years of primary school, after pre-primary. Children build strong reading, writing and counting, and learn by doing, playing and exploring the world around them. Search words: Grade 1, Grade 2, Grade 3, Class 1–3, early years, KEYA, assessment number.

children.note: The stage that follows PP1 and PP2.
Lower primary is three years: Grade 1, Grade 2 and Grade 3.

manas.q: Which grades make up lower primary?

children.note: The 2019 curriculum framework says children enter Grade 1 at about six years old. Check your school's admission rules.

manas.q: At about what age do children start Grade 1?

children.note: Children arrive from two years of pre-primary, where they learnt through play. Grade 1 builds gently on that.

manas.q: What comes just before Grade 1?

children.note: Pre-primary and lower primary together make up Early Years Education in the CBC structure.

manas.q: Which two levels make up Early Years Education?

children.note: Children learn through activities, songs, games, stories and real objects, not only by copying from the board.
One map for Grade 1 alone: the weekly timetable (31 lessons), each learning area's themes and strands, rubric levels and home ideas, from KICD's revised designs.
KICD's Grade 1–3 page lists nine learning areas. Names below are the official ones.
Children listen, speak, read and write in English: sounds, words, short stories, and simple sentences about daily life.

manas.q: What is the English learning area called in Grades 1–3?

children.note: Watoto husikiliza, huzungumza, husoma na kuandika kwa Kiswahili: hadithi, nyimbo na sentensi fupi.
Counting, numbers, adding and taking away, shapes, measuring and money. Course books call it Mathematical Activities.

manas.q: Which learning area covers counting, shapes and money?

children.note: Exploring home, school and nature: weather, plants, animals, water, keeping clean and staying safe.

manas.q: Which learning area explores weather, plants and water?

children.note: Drawing, colouring, modelling, music, singing, dance and movement games that grow imagination and healthy bodies.

manas.q: Which learning area covers art, music and movement?

children.note: Learning in the language of the local community, through stories, songs and talk, to value home language and culture.

manas.q: Which learning area uses the local community language?

children.note: Christian Religious Education: Bible stories, prayer, and values like love, kindness and sharing.

manas.q: What does CRE stand for?

children.note: Islamic Religious Education: stories, short surahs, prayer and good manners taught in Islam.

manas.q: What does IRE stand for?

children.note: Hindu Religious Education: stories, festivals, prayer and values from the Hindu faith.
Strong reading and writing in two languages is a big goal of these years.
Children learn letter sounds, blend them into words, and read short words aloud.
They read simple stories and answer questions about what happened and why.
From tracing letters to writing their name, then short sentences about home and friends.
Show-and-tell, news time and retelling stories help children speak clearly.
English and Kiswahili are both learnt, so children can read and talk in both.
Maths starts with real things children can touch and count.
Counting objects, reading and writing numbers, and putting them in order.
Simple sums using bottle tops, beans or sticks before written work.
Spotting circles, squares and triangles around the home, and making patterns.
Comparing long and short, heavy and light, full and empty, using everyday items.
Recognising Kenyan coins and notes, and pretend buying and selling.

manas.q: Which everyday trip is good for practising money skills?

children.note: Days of the week, morning and evening, and simple daily routines.
Language of the home matters in the early grades.
Children understand new ideas faster when they first hear them in a familiar language.
Grandparents' stories, riddles and songs are rich learning in the indigenous language.
This depends on the school and community. Check with your school.
Art, music and play are real learning, not extras.
Drawing, painting, and making things with clay, paper or waste materials.
Songs, rhymes and traditional dances build memory, rhythm and teamwork.
Running, jumping, skipping and ball games build strong, healthy bodies.
Earlier designs had a separate hygiene and nutrition area; today such topics appear within other areas.

manas.q: Is Hygiene and Nutrition still listed as a separate Grade 1–3 area?

children.note: Families choose one religious education option, depending on what the school offers.
KICD lists CRE, IRE and HRE for Grades 1–3.

manas.q: Which three religious education options are listed for Grades 1–3?

children.note: Ask the school which options it offers and tell them your family's choice.
All options teach respect, honesty, kindness and caring for others.
Much learning happens away from the desk.
Making a chart of the weather, growing beans in a tin, or building a model home.
Planting and watering seeds teaches science, care and patience.
Looking at trees, insects, soil and water sources near the school.
Working in pairs and groups helps children share, listen and solve problems together.
Bottle tops, stones and leaves make cheap counting and art materials.
CBC builds skills and values, not just facts.
The framework names seven, including communication and collaboration, critical thinking and problem solving, and creativity and imagination.

manas.q: How many core competencies does CBC name?

children.note: Telling news, asking questions and listening to others in class.
Trying again after a mistake, and asking 'why?' and 'how?'.
Where available, simple safe use of devices with adult guidance. Check with your school.
Taking turns, caring for books, and greeting others politely.

manas.q: Name two CBC values young children practise daily.

children.note: Telling the truth and helping a classmate who is hurt or sad.
Teachers watch, listen and check work through the year.
Teachers check learning day by day through observation, questions, oral reading and short tasks.

manas.q: What is day-to-day checking of learning by the teacher called?

children.note: Teachers see whether a child can actually do a skill, like reading aloud or counting money.
Samples of a child's work may be kept to show progress over time. Ask your school how it does this.
Schools share progress with parents. Ask the teacher how and when.

KICD's 2019 timeline shows a national assessment at the end of Grade 3. KNEC's list of school assessments names a Kenya Early Years Assessment (KEYA). Ask your school what is done in Grade 3 and when.

manas.q: At the end of which grade does KICD's timeline show the first national assessment?

children.note: KNEC's regulations list the Kenya Early Years Assessment (KEYA) among its school assessments, alongside KPSEA (Grade 6) and KJSEA (Grade 9). (KNEC, read 4 Nov 2026 — check the current rule.)
KNEC says the assessment number a learner gets at Grade 3 is their unique identifier up to Grade 12. Write it down and keep it with the birth certificate.

manas.q: What number given in Grade 3 follows a learner to Grade 12?

children.note: KNEC also runs a Grade 3 monitoring study of learning achievement (NASMLA) in sampled schools; it is a national check, not a result for your child.
Assessment in these years aims to find where a child needs help, so worry less and support more.
Parents are partners in CBC learning.
Often a small activity: collect leaves, count items at home, or ask a grandparent a question.

children.topic: Help, don't do it for them
children.note: Guide and encourage, but let the child do the work and make mistakes.
Use old boxes, bottle tops, seeds and newspaper for projects. Ask the teacher if unsure what is needed.
Visit or message the teacher about how your child is doing and how to help.
Count steps, plates or chapatis together; a market trip is a maths lesson.
Regular sleep, a good breakfast and a quiet homework corner help children learn.
Ten minutes of reading together each day makes a big difference.
Read stories to your child, then let them read to you.
Read in English, Kiswahili and your home language.
Ask: what happened? How did they feel? What would you do?
Signs, labels, newspapers and matatu stickers are reading practice too.
Family stories, riddles and songs grow vocabulary just as well.
Community and school libraries lend books for free or at low cost. Check what is near you.
After Grade 3, children move to upper primary.
Upper primary is Grade 4 to Grade 6, part of Middle School.

manas.q: Which grades come after lower primary?

children.note: Activity-based areas grow into subjects such as Science and Technology, Social Studies and Agriculture.

manas.q: Name a new learning area that appears in Grade 4.

children.note: Children are expected to read and write more independently.
Keep the reading habit, practise times tables and build curiosity.

nodeData.topic: Grade 1 — the first year of primary
nodeData.note: Draft · review in progress. Grade 1 in detail, from KICD's revised Grade 1–3 designs (2024), read on 25 Nov 2026: what each learning area covers this year, the weekly timetable, how teachers assess, and how parents can help. Search words: Grade 1, class one, darasa la kwanza, gredi ya 1, lower primary, early years, standard one.

children.note: The first of the three lower-primary years, straight after PP2.
Grade 1 starts lower primary (Grades 1–3). Together with PP1 and PP2 it belongs to the early years stage.

manas.q: Which stage of CBC does Grade 1 belong to?

children.note: Children arrive from two years of play-based pre-primary. Grade 1 builds on the same themes: greetings, family, home and school.
The 2019 framework puts Grade 1 entry at about six years. Admission rules can change, so confirm with the school.
KICD reviewed and cut down the number of learning areas in 2024. The Grade 1 designs used here are those revised versions.

manas.q: When were the Grade 1–3 designs last revised?

children.note: The whole Grade 1–3 picture: learning areas, reading at home, assessment and moving to Grade 4.
KICD sets the number of lessons per week for each learning area in lower primary.
All learning areas together make 31 lessons a week in Grades 1–3, including one pastoral or religious instruction lesson.

manas.q: How many lessons a week does a Grade 1 learner have?

children.note: Art, music and movement get the biggest share of the week — play and making things are real learning at this age.

manas.q: Which learning area has the most lessons in Grade 1?

children.note: English Language Activities and Mathematical Activities each get five lessons a week.
Kiswahili (or Kenya Sign Language for deaf learners) and Environmental Activities get four lessons each.
Three lessons a week for the family’s chosen option: CRE, IRE or HRE.
Two lessons a week in the language of the school’s area.
One lesson a week for the pastoral or religious instruction programme, separate from Religious Education.
The Grade 1–3 timetable page gives lessons per week, not minutes. Ask your school how long each lesson is.
Listening, speaking, reading and writing in English through 15 everyday themes.
Listening and Speaking, Reading, Language Use, and Writing — about 150 lessons in the year.

manas.q: What are the four strands of Grade 1 English?

children.note: Each theme targets a group of letters and their sounds, starting with a to h, so children can read 2–3 letter words.
KICD asks teachers not to use terms like “noun” or “verb” in Grades 1–3. Children pick up sentence patterns by using them.

manas.q: Are grammar terms taught by name in Grade 1?

children.note: Children learn how to sit, hold a book, turn pages and follow words with a finger.
Pre-writing, handwriting, spelling, simple punctuation and guided writing of short sentences.
Greetings, School, Family, Home, Time, Weather and our environment, Hygiene, Parts of the body.

manas.q: Name three of the Grade 1 English themes.

children.note: My friends, Safety, Community leaders, Living together, Technology, Numbers, Conserving resources.
English becomes the main language of teaching from Grade 4, so the early years lay its foundation.
Read short texts of about 200 words fluently and with understanding, and write simple sentences neatly.
Kusikiliza, kuzungumza, kusoma na kuandika kupitia mada kumi za maisha ya kila siku.
Kiswahili is Kenya’s national and official language; most children learn it as a second language.
Darasani, Familia, Tarakimu, Siku za wiki, Mimi na wenzangu, Mwili wangu, Usafi wa mwili, Vyakula vyetu, Jikoni, Michezo.

manas.q: Taja mada tatu za Kiswahili Gredi ya 1.

children.note: First lessons: maamkuzi na maagano — Hujambo? Sijambo; Kwaheri ya kuonana — practised in pairs and groups.
Some activities ask the child to discuss greetings with a parent or guardian, linking class to home.
The timetable lists Kenya Sign Language Activities in the same slot for deaf learners.
Numbers, measurement and simple geometry with real objects — about 150 lessons.
The year opens with pre-number work: grouping things by size, colour, shape, use and texture, and making patterns.

manas.q: What does Grade 1 maths start with?

children.note: Count forward to 50 and back from 30; read and write numbers 1–50 in figures and 1–10 in words.

manas.q: Up to which number do Grade 1 learners count forward?

children.note: Using + and =; adding two or three single digits; adding a 2-digit and a 1-digit number with no carrying, total up to 50.
Using − and =; taking away single digits, and a 1-digit number from a 2-digit number with no borrowing.
Comparing longer/shorter, heavier/lighter, more/less, and measuring with everyday units like hand spans or cups.
Naming the days of the week and months of the year, and linking days to activities.
Kenyan coins (sh.1, 5, 10, 20 and 40) and the sh.50 note; buying up to two items with no change needed.

manas.q: Which note do Grade 1 learners learn to recognise?

children.note: Straight and curved lines; rectangles, triangles and circles in the world around them, and patterns with shapes.
Wanjiru has 23 beans and gets 4 more: 23 + 4 = 27. No carrying needed — exactly the Grade 1 level.
Hygiene, home, school, weather, soil, water, plants and animals — about 120 lessons.
Social Environment, Natural Environment, and Resources in our Environment.

manas.q: What are the three strands of Grade 1 Environmental Activities?

children.note: Washing face, teeth, hands, feet and hair with local materials, including practising tooth brushing.
Keeping the home clean, common accidents at home and practising safe road crossing.
Basic needs, food from plants and animals, and choosing food for a healthy body.
Landmarks between home and school, staying safe on the way, and the local market.
Watching the sky and weather, exploring soil, and noticing sounds around us.
Saving water, edible and non-edible plants, a kitchen garden, and caring for domestic animals.
The class CSL activity is run through Environmental Activities. See the CSL branch below.
Music, art and craft, and movement — about 210 lessons, the largest area.
Creating and Executing, Performing and Displaying, and Appreciation.

manas.q: What three art forms does Creative Activities cover?

children.note: Jumping, stretching, throwing and catching, log roll and T-balances — building strong, coordinated bodies.
Drawing, painting and colouring, pattern making, paper craft and modelling.
Rhythm, melody, Kenyan singing games, action songs, percussion instruments and listening to musical sounds.
A Grade 1 sub-strand on staying safe around water.

manas.q: Which safety topic is part of Grade 1 Creative Activities?

children.note: KICD bases it on learning by doing: exploring, creating and performing, linked to the child’s own culture.
Two lessons a week in the language of the school’s catchment area.
Taught in the local community language, building pride in culture and a base for learning a second language.

manas.q: Which indigenous language does a Grade 1 class learn?

children.note: Listening and Speaking, Reading, and Writing — 20 lessons each in the year.
Family member names, greetings at home, and items found at home, through songs, rhymes and pictures.
Stories, riddles and songs from grandparents fit this area well. Ask your child what they learnt.
Families choose CRE, IRE or HRE — 90 lessons in the year, three a week.
Christian RE: creation, the Bible (Joseph, the chariot of fire), Jesus’ early life, values like sharing, obedience, honesty and thankfulness, and the church.

manas.q: Name the three religious education options in Grade 1.

children.note: Islamic RE: Arabic alphabet and short surahs, hadith on obeying parents and cleanliness, pillars, wudhu, good manners and the Eids.
Hindu RE: creation and the five elements (panchmahabhoot), names of Paramatma, scriptures and stories, worship and festivals, sadachaar (good conduct), and simple yoga.
All three build values such as respect, honesty, sharing and care for others and the environment.
One whole-class service activity a year, planned by the class teacher.
Children connect what they learn to real life by doing a small, safe activity within the school.
Preparation, doing the activity, then reflecting: what went well, what did not, what to change.

manas.q: What are the three steps of a CSL activity?

children.note: One integrated activity each year, with themes that change; parents are partners in planning it.
Teachers assess groups on skills, core competencies and values, using checklists or observation.
Every lesson names the skills and values it builds.
Example from English: using new greeting words outside class.
Example from Maths: making patterns with real objects.
Example from Maths: helping to arrange items at home by size and colour.
Working together and waiting patiently for a turn during greetings practice.
Taking care of reading books and helping to keep things tidy at home.
Self-esteem, safety and social cohesion are woven into lessons rather than taught separately.
Classroom assessment only — no national exam in Grade 1.
Designs use a rubric: Exceeds Expectations, Meets Expectations, Approaches Expectations, Below Expectations.

manas.q: What are the four rubric levels used in Grade 1?

children.note: Meets Expectations: finds missing numbers in patterns up to 20. Approaches: up to 15. Below: up to 10, partly right.
Oral questions, watching children work, and portfolios of their work.
The first KNEC school assessment comes at the end of Grade 3 (KEYA). Check details with your school.
Cheap, everyday ideas tied to what Grade 1 learns.
Practise morning and evening greetings in English, Kiswahili and your home language.
Let your child count tomatoes or coins; buy two items with exact money.
Sorting socks by colour and size is real Grade 1 maths.
A simple routine that matches the Cleaning My Body lessons.
Sing the days of the week and talk about what happens on each one.
KICD’s parent guidelines ask parents to follow homework through the school diary.
Grade 2 continues the same learning areas at a higher level.
Same learning areas and timetable; numbers and reading go further. See the Lower primary map.
End of lower primary, the first KNEC assessment and the learner’s assessment number.
